title: Prioritise AI Use Cases for a Large Enterprise
subtitle: Choose a defensible enterprise AI portfolio with gates, adoption-adjusted value and evidence-based waves.
author: By Sourav Banerjee

practice_prompts.label: What 'prioritise' decides
practice_prompts.hint: Pilot or portfolio, sponsor, budget, risk appetite, past attempts, build or buy; state the insurer assumptions.

practice_prompts.label: Cards, gates and weights
practice_prompts.hint: The card fields, the four gates and their dispositions, seven weights with a reason each.

practice_prompts.label: Value and the stress test
practice_prompts.hint: Rebuild #7's $1.9M; name the five ways the sum breaks and which items are decided.

practice_prompts.label: Platform, waves and kill criteria
practice_prompts.hint: Enablers funded with wave 1, what each wave proves, who signs each stage.

practice_prompts.label: The pet project and the cost pivot
practice_prompts.hint: Four evidence-gated steps to #29; cost per use case to production.

rubric: I refused to pick the most impressive demo and said why its production cost is hidden.
I asked whether the decision is one pilot or a funded portfolio, and stated assumptions when unanswered.
I turned ideas into one card and applied the four gates before any score.
I stated seven weights aloud with reasons, and estimated value as volume × saving × unit cost × adoption with run cost subtracted.
I named compensation, dependencies, double counting, false precision and monoculture, and said only items stable under reweighting are decided.
I funded the gateway, evaluation harness, ingestion and retrieval with wave 1 rather than ranking them as use cases.
I sequenced waves by what each proves and wrote kill criteria with signers before the pilot.
I turned the executive's favourite into a destination with evidence gates instead of a refusal.
I named people time as the dominant cost and cost per use case to production as the metric.

editorial_review.evidence: Compared all 27 captured sections of the insurer prioritisation case against the previous casebook item by item and split them into 61 coverage rows. The previous version kept every table and figure but had thinned the prose: it dropped the verbatim prompt, the 'avoid the most impressive demo' quote, the six first-pick properties as a list, the source's spoken framing, the 'two-week clock' quote, the reasons for the weights, the gap explanation for the $5M slide, the figure-explanation text for the platform (gateway controls, ingestion inputs, retrieval scope), wave 1's 'no headline' rationale, the 'portfolio only grows' kill-criteria rationale, the accelerator reuse rate, the executive script, the two-minute spoken answer, 'cache safely' and the cost-complaint rule; it also contradicted the source's 'no deep background' assumption and softened the US rate-filing fact. All restored. Recomputed all thirty weighted scores (all match) and the $1,890,000 estimate. The brief now opens on the thirty-idea problem, defines card, gate, enabler, wave, kill criteria and SME, and traces #7 through the method because the vocabulary is otherwise unfamiliar. Added, and labelled as added: a filled #7 card, three scoring drills, three changed-constraint exercises, and a numbers table in Quick review. Source inconsistencies resolved in text (2026-11-16): bucket rules never placed a score under 2.6 → added rule 6 'a score under 2.6 is No', matching #24 (2.05, No) and the bucket totals; executive script's 'in four months' for settlement recommendations → dates from the source's own wave plan (claims summaries within eight months, #29 recommendations in shadow from month fourteen), since the wave table and #29 route are the consistent majority.
